items.title: Building Strength and Trust: Procurement’s Role in Creating Organisational Confidence
items.author: Lars_Elmquist
items.text: Procurement is often measured by savings, but its real influence comes from something harder to quantify: trust. Inspired by a recent event in Copenhagen's Carlsberg Byen, where the iconic elephants symbolise strength and trust, this article explores how procurement can build both across the organisation. Through competence, collaboration and candour, teams earn the credibility to shape decisions earlier. It also examines how SAP Ariba and AI can strengthen insight while keeping accountability and trust firmly human.

items.title: Blog 8 - SAP ESM for HR - Roles, Permissions, and Identity: The Security Layer Nobody Talks About
items.author: andreamazzanti
items.text:
The Most Underestimated Configuration Area in Any ESM Implementation 
 Ask any experienced ESM consultant what generates the most support tickets on go-live day, and the answer is almost always the same: access and permissions. An employee cannot see the self-service portal. An HR agent can log in but cannot view cases. A supervisor can see cases but cannot reassign them. A system administrator cannot access configuration settings. 
 None of these are product defects. They are the predictable result of a security and identity model that was not fully designed, mapped, and tested before go-live. 
 The reason this happens so often is that the security layer in SAP ESM for HR is not a single configuration screen in a single system. It spans four interconnected layers: SAP SuccessFactors, SAP IPS, SAP IAS, and SAP ESM. Every layer must be configured correctly and connected to the others for any user to experience what they are supposed to experience. 
 This post explains each layer, how they connect, and how to design the whole model before touching a single configuration screen. 
 The identity and access model for SAP ESM for HR works as a chain. Each step of the chain depends on the one before it. A break at any point in the chain means the user either cannot access the system or does not see what they should see. 
 Layer 1 — SAP SuccessFactors EC Permission Roles 
 This is considered the source system. What the user is authorised to do and see within the SuccessFactors ecosystem. 
 Layer 2 — SAP IPS (Identity Provisioning Service) 
 How the user's identity is authenticated and which group they belong to for access provisioning purposes. I PS reads employee identity attributes from SF EC using the sf. user.attributes query and transforms them into SCIM payloads consumed by IAS. 
 Layer 3 — SAP IAS (Identity Authentication Service) 
 IAS then manages the user account used for Single Sign-On (SSO) login into SAP ESM and controls business role assignments. The ESM business role assignment is managed via IAS application groups synchronization with two steps: 
 SAP IPS assigns IAS group based on SF EC employee attributes (Organization Unit, Reference Role and Team Member Size) 
 SAP IPS synchronizes IAS group members with SAP ESM business roles members 
 Layer 4 — SAP ESM (Users and Business Roles) 
 What the user can see and do within the ESM platform: the cases, the configuration, the agent workspace, the analytics. 
 Think of it as a pipeline: SuccessFactors establishes who the person is and what they are authorised to do in the HR system. IAS authenticates them and groups them. IPS provisions their access to the technical components. ESM assigns them a functional role. All four must be aligned. 
 SAP SuccessFactors Permission Roles 
 SAP SuccessFactors uses a Role-Based Permission (RBP) model to control access to all SuccessFactors functionality, including the parts of SuccessFactors which are visible to ESM users, the employee profile data, and the HR process tiles. For an ESM for HR implementation, the SuccessFactors administrator must configure permission roles that cover three specific things: 
 Access to employee self-service functionality: Employees need permission to access the HR Service tile (or equivalent entry point) from the SuccessFactors Home Page. Without this permission, the employee sees no route into the ESM self-service portal from SuccessFactors. 
 HR agent access to SuccessFactors data within ESM: When HR agents view an employee's SuccessFactors profile from within the ESM agent workspace, they are accessing SuccessFactors data through an embedded view. The data they can see is governed by their SuccessFactors permission role, not by their ESM business role. An HR agent with a narrow SuccessFactors permission role will see a narrow profile. A Payroll specialist who needs compensation data must have a SuccessFactors permission role that includes it. 
 The practical implication: SuccessFactors permission role design is not solely an HR system task. It directly affects what HR agents can see when they access the SF Employee People Profile via ESM. 
 SAP IPS and IAS 
 SAP IAS authenticates users, confirming who they are, and organises them into user groups that are then mapped to roles in ESM. When a user logs into SuccessFactors and navigates to the HR service portal, IAS handles the Single Sign-On (SSO) handshake, confirming their identity to ESM without requiring a separate login. From the user's perspective, the experience is seamless. From a configuration perspective, the SSO trust relationship between SuccessFactors, IAS, and ESM must be explicitly established and tested. 
 Beyond authentication, IAS manages user provisioning through user groups. These groups are the bridge between who someone is (their SuccessFactors identity) and what they can do (their ESM role). The groups you define in IAS must map precisely to the business roles you define in ESM and the role assignments you configure in IPS. 
 Typical IAS user groups for an ESM for HR implementation: 
 IAS User Groups and their purpose. 
 ESM-Employees & Managers: Employees with access to the self-service widget 
 ESM-HRAgents: HR agents with access to the agent workspace and case management 
 ESM-HRSupervisors: Team leads with access to case reassignment and team queues 
 ESM-HRManagers: HR managers with visibility across team performance and SLA reporting 
 ESM-Administrators: System administrators with access to configuration and system settings 
 The names and groupings above are illustrative — your implementation will define its own group structure. What matters is that the groups are defined before ESM business roles are configured, because the mapping runs in that direction: IAS groups first, ESM roles second. 
 SAP ESM Business Roles 
 SAP ESM business roles define what a user can see and do within the ESM platform itself. They control access to workspaces, case types, queues, configuration areas, analytics, and knowledge base management. The five standard ESM business roles and what each one enables: 
 Employee (Self-Service User) 
 The most populated role: every employee in scope. Employees can access the self-service widget, browse the knowledge base, create cases, view their own case history, and communicate with HR through the case thread. They cannot see other employees' cases, access agent workspaces, or view configuration. 
 HR Agent 
 The operational core of the HR SSC. HR agents can view and manage the cases assigned to their team queue, update case status, respond to employees, create internal notes, view the SuccessFactors employee profile in context, and access knowledge base articles. They cannot reassign cases outside their team, access SLA management settings, or view other teams' queues — unless specifically configured. 
 HR Supervisor / Team Lead 
 Supervisors have everything an HR agent has, plus the ability to view and reassign cases across their team, monitor queue volumes and SLA status for their team, and access team-level performance dashboards. This role is critical for SLA management and escalation handling. It is the role that acts when a case is approaching breach. 
 HR Manager / SSC Manager 
 Managers have read access across multiple teams and visibility into cross-team analytics, SLA compliance reports, and case volume trends. They do not manage individual cases day-to-day but need the visibility to manage SSC performance and make resourcing decisions. 
 System Administrator 
 The administrator role has access to all ESM configuration: case types, service catalog, routing rules, SLA definitions, knowledge base management, channel configuration, and user management. This role should be tightly controlled: broad configuration access in the wrong hands is how service catalogs get accidentally modified, and routing rules get broken. 
 The most useful way to think about this model is as a chain of mappings. Each layer hands off to the next: SAP SuccessFactors EC Users attributes are read via SAP IPS -> SAP IPS assigns IAS group based on SAP SuccessFactors EC Users attributes -> SAP IPS synchronizes IAS group members with SAP ESM business roles members -> as a result, users are created and assigned to their respective SAP ESM Business Roles. 
 A user's experience in ESM is the product of all these mappings being correct. If any link in the chain is broken or incomplete, the user will either be blocked entirely or will have an incomplete and confusing experience. 
 Common Configuration Mistakes 
 Mistake 1: Configuring ESM roles before IAS groups are defined 
 The configuration sequence matters. IAS user groups must exist before ESM business roles can be mapped to them. Teams that configure ESM roles first and then try to retrofit IAS groups create mismatches that are time-consuming to diagnose and fix. 
 Mistake 2: Treating all HR agents as identical 
 HR agents in different teams often need different levels of data visibility in SuccessFactors. A Benefits specialist does not need to see payroll data. A Payroll specialist should not have access to employee relations case notes. Designing a single "HR Agent" SuccessFactors permission role for all agents creates either over-exposure or under-exposure. Define SuccessFactors permission roles at the team level, not the platform level. 
 Mistake 3: Testing SSO with administrator accounts only 
 SSO testing with administrator accounts will pass even when the configuration has gaps — administrator roles typically have broad access that masks edge cases. Test SSO and portal access with representative accounts from each user type: a standard employee, an HR agent, a supervisor, and a manager. Each will expose different gaps. 
 Mistake 4: Not planning for employee offboarding 
 When an employee leaves the organisation, their SuccessFactors account is deactivated. If IAS provisioning is correctly configured, that deactivation flows through to IAS and then to ESM — the employee's self-service access is revoked automatically. If it is not correctly configured, departed employees retain portal access. Verify the offboarding flow explicitly as part of integration testing. 
 Roles and Permissions Readiness Checklist 
 Before going live, confirm all of the following: 
 [ ] SuccessFactors permission roles are defined for each user type, including the Integration Suite service account 
 [ ] IAS user groups are created and mapped to SuccessFactors user populations 
 [ ] SSO trust is established between SuccessFactors, IAS, and ESM — tested with non-administrator accounts 
 [ ] ESM business roles are created and mapped to IAS user groups 
 [ ] Every user type has been tested end-to-end: login → correct workspace → correct data visibility 
 [ ] HR agent data visibility has been validated by teams: Payroll agents see payroll data; Benefits agents see benefits data; cross-team visibility is blocked where intended 
 [ ] Employee offboarding flow has been tested: deactivated SuccessFactors account loses ESM portal access 
 [ ] System administrator access is restricted to named individuals and documented 
 What Comes Next 
 With routing, SLAs, integration, and identity all designed and configured, your ESM for HR implementation is taking shape. The next phase is making sure it all works before your employees and HR agents encounter it for the first time. 
 Next post: Blog 9 — UAT: How to Test SAP ESM for HR Before You Go Live 
 Part of the series: "Implementing SAP ESM for HR — A Practitioner's Guide from Zero to Go-Live." All content is based on hands-on implementation experience and SAP best practice materials.

items.title: Eclipse 2026-06 Update Issue Leading to a Broken Installation
items.author: MariaMueller
items.text:
Since Eclipse 2026-09 has been published, a new issue came up where updating Eclipse 2026-06 or installing ABAP development tools for Eclipse can leave Eclipse in an unusable state . The installation will succeed, but the affected installations fail to start again due to dependency conflicts involving different versions of the org.objectweb.asm library. 
 We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience this may cause. We understand that a broken IDE is causing disruptions in development activities. Please help us in making other ADT users aware of this issue and how to avoid it. 

 The root cause 
 The root cause lies in the Eclipse update mechanism itself. After the release of Eclipse 2026-09, Eclipse pulls newer dependencies of org.objectweb.asm into the 2026-06 installation, resulting in incompatible bundle versions. As this is caused by the underlying Eclipse platform, we cannot fix the issue from the ADT side. 
 For more information on this, please find the following issues: https://github.com/eclipse-equinox/p2/issues/1119 and https://github.com/eclipse-platform/eclipse.platform.ui/issues/4328 . 

 How to avoid and recommended solution 
 In case you have an existing installation of Eclipse 2026-06 and there is an update for the tools, please follow these instructions to avoid broken Eclipse installation: 
 Open your existing Eclipse installation and do not follow the automated update pop-up. 
 Open "Help" -> "Install New Software". Click on Manage and deactivate the update site "SAP Development Tools" (e.g. https://tools.hana.ondemand.com/2026-06 or https://tools.hana.ondemand.com/latest ) by unchecking the box in the table. 

 Click on "Help" -> "Check for Updates" and do the update to Eclipse 2026-09. 
 After successful update to Eclipse 2026-09, you can activate the "SAP Development Tools" update site with for example https://tools.hana.ondemand.com/latest again and do the ADT update by using "Help" -> "Check for Updates". 
 Re-use your existing workspace to keep your ABAP projects and other data. 
 If you have a broken installation, the recommended approach is a fresh installation of Eclipse 2026-09 together with the latest ADT version . This is currently the simplest and most reliable recovery option and with re-using the workspace, you will keep all your data! 

 Further references 
 Please see also note 3806264 . It also describes how to install the tools into Eclipse 2026-06.

items.title: SAP BPA RDP: Why We Need Remote Desktop Execution for Scalable Automation
items.author: Vennilla00
items.text:
Introduction 
 A few months ago, I was working on a SAP Build Process Automatio n (BPA) project that started small — just a handful of users running an Excel-driven automation , worked on my machine, on the test users' machines, and even during the pilot. Then came rollout. 
 The user base jumped from 20 to a few hundred, with plans to reach 1000+. Suddenly, the i nstall the SAP Desktop Agent on every machine model didn't feel so simple anymore. Some laptops had restricted admin rights, Some users worked outside the company. Every failure ticket had a different root cause agent not running, Excel version mismatch, SSO token expired, machine asleep at scheduled run time. 
 That's when we made the call: stop running automations on user desktops, and move them to an RDP / VM-based execution model. 
 A second Use-case: 
 Requirement: We need an automation that picks up a file and processes it every day at 12:00 AM, 12:00 PM, 3:00 AM, and 3:00 PM . 
 Simple enough — BPA has a built-in timer trigger for exactly this. I built it, tested it and scheduled it on my local agent. 
 Then the reality check. 
 At 3:00 AM, my laptop was off. At 12:00 AM, it was asleep. When I opened it in the morning, BPA happily triggered the job — several hours late. 
 Here's the thing nobody tells you when you first start with BPA schedulers: 
 T he timer runs in the cloud, but the automation runs on the agent. 
 If the agent (your laptop) is off, locked, or disconnected, the trigger just queues up and waits. 
 So a 3:00 AM job on a developer's laptop is basically a 9:00 AM job whenever the developer walks in. 
 This is exactly the kind of scenario where an RDP / VM-based agent shines: 
 The VM is always on . 
 The VM is always logged in (under a technical user). 
 The VM is always connected to BPA. 
 The timer fires at 3:00 AM → the VM picks it up at 3:00 AM. Done. 
 After moving that automation to the VM, the scheduled runs became reliable — which is exactly what you want from a scheduled job. 
 What is RDP in this context? 
 In simple terms: instead of the automation running on each end user's laptop, it runs on a centrally managed virtual machine where the SAP Desktop Agent is installed once. Users don't need the agent — they just trigger the process (via a Fiori form, workflow task, or API), and the VM does the heavy lifting. 
 Workflow Vs Automation 
 Workflow → runs in the cloud, no agent needed. 
 Automation → touches Excel, SAP GUI, PDFs, Outlook → needs an agent → needs a machine. 
 Once we accepted that automations always need a machine somewhere , the question became: whose machine? Every user's, or one VM we control? 
 RDP is a solution where the automation runs on a virtual machine (VM) instead of on each user’s personal desktop. In this model, the user does not need to install the agent on their local machine. Instead, the automation is triggered and executed in the VM environment, which is centrally managed. 
 This is especially useful when: 
 many users need access to the same automation 
 the process must run consistently without depending on a user’s local machine 
 the user machine is not always available or is restricted by security policies 
 you want to reduce installation and maintenance effort 
 What worked well for us 
 Here's what genuinely made life easier after the switch: 
 1. One agent to maintain, not hundreds. 
 Patching, version upgrades, and Excel/Outlook compatibility issues went from "coordinate with IT for 500 machines" to "log into the VM and fix it once." 
 2. Runs even when the user is offline. 
 This was huge. Users would trigger a process at end of day, log off, and go home. The VM continued executing overnight. Previously, the automation would freeze the moment their laptop went to sleep. 
 3. Cleaner authorization model. 
 We use a technical user for backend calls on the VM. No more chasing individual user role assignments across S/4HANA. 
 The challenges nobody warned us about 
 This is the part I wish someone had written a blog about before we started. So here it is. Challenge 1: SSO doesn't behave the way you think in a VM 
 Our first big surprise. The automation was calling a BAPI via the SAP GUI script, and it kept failing with authorization errors — even though the same script worked perfectly on a user's laptop. 
 The reason: the VM agent runs under a service/technical account , not the actual end user's SSO context. SSO ticket propagation simply doesn't work the way it does on a user's own desktop session. 
 What we did: switched BAPI-based calls to Basic Authentication with a technical user , and for anything customer-facing, moved to OData actions instead of GUI scripting. Cleaner, faster, and doesn't depend on GUI at all. Challenge 2: Agent disconnects at the worst possible time 
 The VM agent occasionally went into a "disconnected" state — usually after Windows updates or network blips. Because we didn't have monitoring on it initially, we only found out when users complained that their tasks were stuck. 
 solution: 
 Added an alert on the BPA agent status. 

 Challenge 3: File and folder access 
 The automation reads Excel files uploaded by users. On a desktop setup, this was easy — the file was already local. On the VM, we had to build an upload path: user uploads via a form → file lands in a shared folder (or SAP Document Management) → VM picks it up. 
 Small architectural change, but it caught us mid-project. 
 Challenge 4: Session locking on the VM 
 If someone RDP into the VM interactively and locked the screen, some automations (especially GUI-based ones) would fail because the desktop session was locked. We ended up disabling interactive login for the technical user during business hours. 
 When to use a Local Desktop Agent vs. an RDP / VM Agent 
 Go with a Local Desktop Agent when: 
 The automation is used by a single user or a very small group (say, < 10 users). 
 The user needs to watch it run or interact with it (attended automation). 
 The trigger is manual — the user clicks a button, opens a form, or launches it from the BPA store. 
 The automation genuinely needs the user's own SSO context (e.g., personal Outlook, personal drives). 
 It's a quick PoC or pilot where you don't want VM infrastructure yet. Go with RDP / VM-based execution when: 
 The automation is scheduled (timer-based): daily, hourly, midnight runs, etc. 
 Many users need to trigger the same automation. 
 The process must run unattended — no one is watching, no one is logged in. 
 You need reliable, predictable runtime independent of any user's laptop. 
 You want centralized monitoring, logging, and error handling . 
 You're connecting to backend systems with a technical user / Basic Auth . 
 You're worried about rollout, patching, or supporting the agent across many machines. 
 Configuration checklist we now use 
 Before going live with any VM-based BPA automation, we run through this list. Sharing it here so you don't have to build one from scratch: 
 VM agent is registered in BPA and shows as connected/healthy 
 Excel, Outlook, SAP GUI, and PDF viewer are installed and licensed on the VM 
 Shared folders / network drives / DMS paths are accessible from the VM 
 Technical user has required S/4HANA / backend role assignments 
 Basic Authentication configured for BAPI-based destinations (not SSO) 
 Session lock policy on the VM is handled (don't let RDP sessions lock during runs) 
 Windows Update / patch window is scheduled outside automation run times 
 Monitoring/alerting on agent status is in place 
 End-to-end test with a real trigger, real file, real user — not just a dev sandbox 
 Not everything in BPA needs an agent. Design your process so that the workflow part (approvals, decisions, notifications) stays in the cloud, and only the desktop-dependent automation part touches the VM. 
 Conclusion 
 Moving to RDP / VM-based execution it was one of the highest-impact changes in the project. It turned a fragile, hard-to-support automation into something we now confidently run for hundreds of users — with a clear path to scaling further. 
 If you're at the point where you're installing the SAP Desktop Agent on your fifth, tenth, or hundredth user machine — pause. Consider whether a VM-based setup would save you months of support pain later. 
 Key takeaways in one line each: 
 Workflow can run agentless. Automation almost always needs an agent — the question is where . 
 One VM > many user desktops, once you cross a small user threshold. 
 Use Basic Auth with a technical user for BAPI calls in VM context. SSO won't behave as expected. 
 Prefer OData actions over GUI scripting wherever possible. 
 This approach makes the process more reliable, scalable, and easier to manage in enterprise environments.

items.text:
How are you troubleshooting data issues in SAP Datasphere without an aDSO-style change log? 
 In SAP BW/4HANA, the aDSO change log is one of our most-used troubleshooting tools. When a report shows wrong numbers or a delta hasn't loaded properly, we go straight to the change log and can see: 
 🔹 Which request brought in a record 
 🔹 The before image and after image of every change 
 🔹 Exactly when a value changed and what it was before 
 🔹 Where the gaps are, by comparing requests against the source 
 In SAP Datasphere, a local table with Delta Capture only keeps the latest version of each record (Change_Type / Change_Date). The internal _Delta table isn't meant for external access, so there's no built-in way to see the old value or trace a change back to a specific load. 
 For those running Datasphere in production (especially with Replication Flows from S/4HANA): 
 1️⃣ How do you investigate a missing or wrong delta record today? 
 2️⃣ Have you built your own change history (append-only history table, SCD Type 2, snapshots)? What worked and what didn't at large volumes? 
 3️⃣ How do you reconcile Datasphere against the source to spot delta gaps?

items.title: The Hidden CPI Bug: When One Record Isn't an Array Anymore
items.author: Mohan-Raj-M
items.text:
Why a Single Item Breaks Your JSON Array in SAP CPI (and How to Fix It) 
 The Problem 
 If you've built a GET API on SAP Integration Suite (CPI) that returns arrays in the JSON response, you've probably run into this classic gotcha: 
 When an element occurs multiple times in the XML, the XML to JSON Converter correctly turns it into a JSON array . 
 When that same element occurs only once , the converter turns it into a plain JSON object instead of a single-item array. 
 This is a huge problem for consuming applications (UI5 apps, external systems, mobile apps, etc.) because they typically expect a consistent data type — always an array — regardless of how many records are returned. If your client code does response.Schedule.ShiftDaysOn.map(...) , it will break the moment there's only one shift day, because ShiftDaysOn is now an object, not an array. 
 This exact issue showed up in an Employee Master API integration flow, where the Schedule node's ShiftDaysOn , ShiftDaysOff , and Holidays fields needed to always render as arrays — even when there was just a single date.

items.title: What’s New in SAP HANA Cloud – September 2026
items.author: thomashammer
items.text:
With the September 2026 release we are continuing to advance SAP HANA Cloud as an intelligent, AI-ready, and enterprise-scale data platform. This quarter introduces innovations that further enable agentic AI scenarios, bring AI closer to data modeling and development, strengthen business continuity, and simplify the management and optimization of enterprise workloads. 

 From SAP Agent Memory Service and enhanced data discovery and retrieval capabilities, to AI-assisted Calculation View modeling, Knowledge Graph Engine innovations, and new performance and administration enhancements, this release makes it easier to build intelligent applications and work with enterprise data. 
 At the same time, new capabilities for multi-region disaster recovery, multitenancy, scalability, and SAP HANA Deployment Infrastructure (HDI) continue to strengthen SAP HANA Cloud as a secure and resilient foundation for business-critical workloads. 
 Whether you’re building agentic AI applications, simplifying data modeling and development, or optimizing and protecting your enterprise data landscape, SAP HANA Cloud continues to provide the foundation for intelligent, scalable, and resilient data management. 
 Let’s take a look at some of the key innovations introduced with the September 2026 release. 
 Agentic AI, Multi-Model & Knowledge Graph Innovations 
 Agent Memory Service for SAP HANA Cloud 
 AI agents that start every session from scratch cannot accumulate knowledge, recall past decisions, or carry user context forward. In QRC3 2026, we address this with the Agent Memory Service powered by SAP HANA Cloud: a managed API service built on SAP CAP that gives agents durable long-term memory and conversation history, backed by the SAP HANA Cloud Vector Engine. 
 Memory entries are scoped by agentID and invokerID, keeping each agent-user pair isolated. The retrieval of past conversations and messages is semantic. Rather than flooding every prompt with an agent's full history, the /v1/memories/search endpoint uses SAP HANA Cloud's VECTOR_EMBEDDING and COSINE_SIMILARITY functions to surface only what is relevant to the current turn, keeping prompts lean and inference costs low. Conversation messages are grouped via /v1/messages for replay and audit. Users retain full oversight, as memory entries can be inspected, edited, or deleted at any time. 
 Agents can now build on accumulated context across sessions, deliver progressively better outcomes, and do so entirely within the SAP HANA Cloud ecosystem. 
 AI_CORE_REQUEST — Call any AI Core Model Directly from SQL 
 Integrating large language models into data workflows has traditionally required application-layer middleware, handling external API calls, separate credential management, and data movement out of and back into the database. In QRC3 2026, AI_CORE_REQUEST removes that overhead entirely. 

 The new SQL function calls any AI Foundation Model registered in SAP AI Core directly from a SELECT statement, accepting a model name, a messages array, and optional inference parameters, and returning the model response as a structured result. AI enrichment, classification, and summarization become inline SQL operations with no external calls from the application tier. Binding AI_CORE_REQUEST to a generated column takes this further. Every insert or update can automatically trigger model inference, keeping AI-derived attributes continuously synchronized with the underlying data with zero additional application code required. 
 The result is AI-powered data pipelines that are architecturally simpler, easier to secure, and fully governed within the database. 
 GeoSPARQL Support in SAP HANA Cloud Knowledge Graph Engine 
 Spatial data - locations, boundaries, distances, routes - is core to logistics, asset management, environmental compliance, and supply chain operations. Until now, combining spatial reasoning with semantic graph queries required two separate engines and architectuarl approaches as well as two separate query languages. In QRC3 2026, the SAP HANA Cloud Knowledge Graph Engine adds GeoSPARQL support , closing that gap. 

 Geometry objects like points, line strings, polygons, can now be stored natively in RDF graphs using standard WKT literals, fully aligned with the OGC GeoSPARQL specification. Spatial functions including intersects, within, contains, distance, and overlaps work directly on graph data and compose naturally with semantic graph traversal in a single SPARQL query. 
 The implementation draws on SAP HANA Cloud's proven spatial engine, so geospatial predicates benefit from the same optimized indexing already used for SQL-based spatial workloads. 
 Data Exploration Tools — Expanded AI Model Support and Calculation View Discovery 
 The Data Exploration Tools in SAP HANA Cloud Central received two meaningful updates in QRC3 2026, making natural language database querying more flexible and more useful for analytics workloads. 
 First, the AI_OBJECT_RETRIEVAL and AI_DATA_RETRIEVAL procedures now support multiple large language models. The MODEL_AND_VERSION parameter accepts both gpt-4.1 (the default) and anthropic--claude-4.6-sonnet , and model selection is exposed directly in the SAP HANA Cloud Central UI when configuring a tool pair. Users choose their preferred model at setup, and that choice is passed to the underlying retrieval procedure at runtime, with no changes required to the SQL procedures themselves. 

 Second, Data Exploration Tools can now include Calculation Views alongside tables, views, and functions. Calculation Views are registered in the Knowledge Graph and RAG table, enabling the AI retrieval layer to discover them, understand their structure, and explain their purpose in response to natural language queries. This brings SAP HANA Cloud's analytic layer like cube models, dimension views, star joins into reach of the same conversational interface already available for relational objects. CATALOG READ privilege is recommended for the dedicated database user to improve query performance, though the tool operates without it. 

 AI-Assisted and Enhanced Calculation View Modeling 
 With Q3 2026, SAP HANA Cloud introduces a range of enhancements that make working with calculation views more intelligent and efficient. New AI-assisted capabilities help developers generate, explain, and optimize expressions using natural-language instructions, while calculation view metadata can now be published to a knowledge graph for AI-assisted discovery and retrieval. Additional modeling enhancements include Debug Mode to identify where specific records are lost, column impact analysis to understand how changes affect a model, dimension labels for clearer identification in analytics tools, and streamlined data preview and search experiences. Together, these updates simplify calculation view development, troubleshooting, and consumption across analytical and AI-driven scenarios. 
 To learn more please check this blogpost by Jan Zwickel. 
 Data Integration 
 SQL on Files: Apache Iceberg format version 3 support 
 Since QRC 3/2025, SAP HANA Cloud has enabled direct read-only access to Apache Iceberg tables in object storage, bringing real-time analytics to Iceberg lakehouses without moving data. That capability has continued to evolve, and with QRC 3/2026 it now extends to Apache Iceberg format version 3, keeping SAP HANA Cloud aligned with the latest open table format standard as the Iceberg ecosystem advances. 
 Format version 3 introduces binary deletion vectors, a more compact way to represent row-level deletes than the position delete files used in version 2. SAP HANA Cloud now reads format version 3 tables that adopt deletion vectors, preserving read correctness on these tables. Note that only the deletion vector capability of format version 3 is supported. Other version 3 features, including variant, geometry, geography, nanosecond-precision timestamps, column default values, and row-level lineage, are not supported. This selective adoption keeps behavior predictable while the broader ecosystem matures around the newer version 3 types. 
 Performance, Scalability & Administration 
 Analytics Advisor 
 Let’s start with an innovation designed to make performance optimization easier: the new Analytics Advisor . 
 For analytical workloads, identifying which queries are responsible for performance issues and determining the right optimization can require significant expertise and manual analysis. 
 The Analytics Advisor helps simplify this process by analyzing multidimensional query performance and identifying slow-running OLAP queries. 
 Partition Advisor 
 Staying with performance optimization, we’re also enhancing the Partition Advisor . 
 Until now, partitioning recommendations have primarily been based on the number of records within a partition. But row count alone doesn’t always provide the complete picture of how large a partition actually is. 
 With this release, the Partition Advisor can also take the actual memory size of partitions into account when generating recommendations. 
 This provides more accurate guidance and helps customers make better-informed partitioning decisions based on the real resource footprint of their data. 
 Support for additional 3 TB in the Memory Performance Class on AWS 
 A new intermediate memory performance instance class is now available on AWS, featuring 3 TB of memory and 185 vCPUs. This addition fills an important gap between the existing 1.8 TB—120 vCPU and 6 TB—440 vCPU instance sizes, providing a meaningful mid-tier option for customers whose workload requirements exceed the capabilities of smaller configurations but do not justify scaling to the largest available tier. 
 The new instance helps right-size infrastructure more effectively by avoiding the need to over-provision resources when additional memory capacity is required. The 3 TB/185 vCPU instance introduces a more balanced alternative, enabling better alignment between workload demands and infrastructure sizing. 
 With a 1:16 memory-to-vCPU ratio, the instance is particularly well suited for SAP HANA Cloud workloads that require a strong balance of compute and memory resources. It provides additional CPU capacity for compute-intensive operations while maintaining a mid-range memory footprint making it an attractive option where scalability and cost efficiency are key considerations. 
 More details about the available options can be found SAP HANA Database Size . 
 Business Continuity & Database Tenant Evolution 
 Supporting Multi-Region Disaster Recovery for Native Multitenancy 
 A regional outage shouldn't put your customers' data out of reach. With SAP HANA Cloud QRC3 we introduce a new Multi-Region Disaster Recovery capability for SAP HANA Cloud Multitenancy instances. It protects the database tenants of an SAP HANA database instance by replicating them, together with the database, to a secondary region. 

 The setup pairs two subaccounts in a BTP region pair, each with a database instance and a hana-multitenancy service instance. While the primary region is active, the secondary holds a passive replica that becomes operational only on failover. While replication is active, tenant data and metadata are continuously replicated asynchronously, meaning that the secondary handles no workload. 
 On failover, the secondary becomes the primay source. All tenants fail over together, and tenant metadata — IDs, access information, lifecycle changes, container references, and labels — is reconstructed so you can manage tenants via the Tenant Management Service REST API. 
 More information can be found in the SAP HANA Cloud online help. 
 Migrating Schemas and HDI Containers to SAP HANA Cloud Database Tenants 
 Already running your multi-tenant application on schemas or HDI containers? You can now transform them in place into full-fledged SAP HANA Cloud database tenants — and unlock tenant-level encryption, recovery, tenant move or copy, and wor

items.title: How AI is Moving from "Helpful Assistant" to Autonomous Workforce Management?
items.author: Fabian_Caelers
items.text:
Hi there and welcome to my latest blog. 
 My name is Fabian Caelers, I have joined the Solution Value Advisory team (SVA) for SAP Fieldglass. Prior to joining I gained extended experience working as part of the SAP Fieldglass Delivery Team, as well as working for an MSP program exclusively for a client. 
 The following three capabilities: enhanced job descriptions, AI-generated SOW descriptions and multilingual translation form the Generative AI foundation of SAP Fieldglass. They are available as company configurations introduced with the 2024.05 release and currently require the SAP AI Unit SKU to access. 
 Generative AI for Job Description Enhancements 
 In the past nearly a quarter of job postings sent to suppliers in past years had job descriptions with 100 characters or less, of course because creating job descriptions is tedious and time-consuming. Those short descriptions caused suppliers to misunderstand job requirements, resulting in unsuitable or underqualified candidates being submitted, extra work for hiring managers, and longer cycle times across the entire hiring process. 
 SAP Fieldglass now leverages Generative AI to produce or enhance more complete and relevant job descriptions. Users retain control over the inputs they provide, including job title, existing job description, and skills and qualification data. Contextual prompts are used to set clear instructions and include safeguard items to avoid unwanted bias. 
 In practical terms, a hiring manager simply lists relevant keywords and clicks Enhance with AI to generate a comprehensive job description. 
 AI-Enhanced SOW Descriptions 
 The same principle applies to Statements of Work. Historically, buyer-supplier collaboration on SOW creation led to at least a 55% increase in cycle times, and vague or incomplete SOWs increased risk for all parties involved. 
 SAP Fieldglass now uses Generative AI to allow users to provide a series of simple inputs and generate a comprehensive SOW description — accelerating the overall SOW collaboration process, reducing cycle times, mitigating project risks, and streamlining operations. 
 AI-Powered Translation Across 21 Languages 
 To ensure job descriptions are clearly understood by regional suppliers, SAP Fieldglass uses AI to simplify translation within the standard workflow. The system automatically detects the language used in the job posting description and translates it to the user's configured profile language. 
 With AI-assisted translations available in 21 languages , companies can support multiple regions and empower global users to swiftly translate job descriptions into their preferred language. The translation uses smart contextual prompt engineering — ensuring that job requirements and responsibilities are accurately conveyed in the target language, not merely translated word for word. After the AI-enhanced translation, users review the content and are able to make any modifications before proceeding. 

 AI-Powered Resume Assessment: The Challenge of High-Volume Hiring 
 When companies face an influx of applications, it becomes difficult to find a starting point — and easy to overlook top candidates, especially as labor shortages and disruptions drive demand for external workers. 
 How AI Resume Assessment Works 
 When the company configuration 'Assess job seeker resumes using AI' is enabled, SAP Fieldglass Contingent Workforce Management uses Machine Learning capabilities to parse through resumes by objectively comparing their contents to keywords provided in the job posting description. 
 Specifically, the feature: 
 Assesses job seekers by matching the skills listed on their resumes to those on the job description. 
 Generates an assessment for each candidate to determine how well their skills and professional experiences align to a job posting. 
 Highlights technical and soft skills on the candidate's resume so hiring managers can see at a glance whether a candidate possesses desired expertise. 
 Joule: The Conversational Layer 
 At the center of this shift is Joule , SAP's AI assistant, now embedded within the SAP Fieldglass experience. Joule provides a conversational experience layer that makes AI practical day to day — allowing users to interact with the system in natural language. 
 A hiring manager can ask Joule how to create a work order and receive a step-by-step guided response, completing the task without navigating menus. An approver who receives a timesheet exception notification can ask Joule what it means and what action is required. A program manager can ask Joule for the current status of open positions or pending approvals. 
 Joule also accelerates job template selection — quickly identifying the best-fit templates and completing known fields with conversational context, minimizing manual input and speeding up job requisition creation. 
 AI-Recommended Worker Roles and Skills Matching 
 New AI features in SAP Fieldglass can automatically recommend relevant worker roles based on the SOW title, description, and historical buyer data. Users review and select these AI-generated suggestions, helping speed up role definition and reduce manual setup during SOW creation. Every decision is automatically logged for audit and compliance. 
 Separately, AI-powered skills matching analyses role descriptions to identify the skills required for each position and matches them against candidate profiles — with SAP estimating this reduces time to source potential candidates by up to 50%, while also reducing unconscious bias in the screening process. 

 The Agentic Shift in Workforce Management 
 Beyond Isolated Features 
 The Generative AI and Machine Learning capabilities described above represent the foundation. But what SAP Fieldglass is now building toward is something more ambitious: agentic AI — experiences that do not merely assist but actively prepare, validate, and progress work across lifecycle steps. 
 This shift is enabled by the strong fundamentals already in place: consistent inputs, reliable guidance, and guardrails that respect templates, permissions, and program rules. 
 The evolution of AI in SAP Fieldglass tells a clear story. It began with Generative AI solving a concrete, painful problem: job descriptions that were too short, too vague, and too slow to produce. It expanded into multilingual translation, SOW generation, and AI-powered resume assessment. And it is now moving into genuinely agentic territory: AI that does not wait to be asked, but actively prepares, validates, and progresses work across the entire external workforce lifecycle. 
 The foundation is already in place. The capabilities are live in production. And the direction is unambiguous: SAP Fieldglass is shifting from a system that helps people do work, to a system that helps work move forward on its own, with people remaining in control of the decisions that matter most. 
 For organizations managing contingent labor and services procurement, the question is no longer whether AI will transform workforce management. It already has. The question now is how quickly your organization is ready to move from "helpful assistant" to autonomous workforce management — and how SAP Fieldglass can help you get there. 
 I hope you like this blog and are looking forward to reading more content soon. 
 Best Regards, 
 Fabian

items.title: What's New in the SAP Fieldglass May 2026 Release
items.author: Fabian_Caelers
items.text:
Hi there and welcome to my latest blog. 
 My name is Fabian Caelers, I have joined the Solution Value Advisory team (SVA) for SAP Fieldglass. Prior to joining I gained extended experience working as part of the SAP Fieldglass Delivery Team, as well as working for an MSP program exclusively for a client. 
 The SAP Fieldglass 2026.05 release marks another significant step forward in SAP's commitment to delivering continuous innovation across external workforce and services procurement management. Please find some of those enhancements highlighted within this blog post. 
 AI-Powered Skills-Based Matching AI-powered skills-based matching now operates significantly faster, enabling hiring managers to describe a role in plain language and receive recommended worker roles based on the description and historical buyer data. This reduces time-to-fill and supports more accurate, skills-aligned sourcing decisions. 
 Resource Revisions: Improved List View, Revision Forms, and Change Visibility SAP Fieldglass has introduced enhancements to improve visibility, usability, and traceability of Resource revisions. Users can now view, sort, and organize Resources by Revision directly from the Resource List View, see newly added custom fields when revising a Resource, and easily identify which fields have changed during a Resource revision that is pending approval. 
 Service Confirmation with Multi-Line Capabilities Suppliers can now itemize multiple event lines into a single Service Confirmation, provided they relate to the same contract, purchase order, and line item. This reduces administrative effort, speeds up approvals, and simplifies end-to-end processing. It also supports smoother integration across SAP Fieldglass, SAP Business Network, and SAP S/4HANA, while remaining compatible with Event Hierarchy workflows. 
 Default Operational Contract Structures Administrators can now start operational contracts using preconfigured defaults, including pick lists and data sets. These standardized structures reduce manual setup, improve accuracy, and provide a consistent foundation for building Event Hierarchies. 
 Admin Changes: Account Category Pick List and Cost Center Buyer administrators can now use a standard SAP Fieldglass account category list and enable only what they need, rather than maintaining custom lists. Custom categories can still be added alongside standard options, improving consistency while maintaining flexibility and reducing administrative effort. 
 Event Hierarchy Enhancements Several targeted improvements have been made to the Event Hierarchy feature within Services Procurement: 
 View and Download Event Hierarchy Custom Lookup Data: Suppliers can now view and download Event Hierarchy custom lookup data maintained by Buyers, including details such as events, billable amounts, sites, and effective dates - improving transparency and alignment on contract terms. 
 Event Itemization Attachments in Attachment Library: Suppliers can add and manage Event Hierarchy attachments directly in the user interface or via the Event Hierarchy Upload connector, keeping relevant documentation organized and accessible. 
 Event-Level Attachment Support in Statement of Work: Buyers can now attach documents directly to specific SOW events, making them visible to Suppliers during review and itemization. This applies to all event types and is also supported through the Attachment XML upload connector. 
 Event Hierarchy Segment Visibility Control for Buyers: Buyers can now control which Event Hierarchy segments are visible for Buyer users on Statements of Work (SOW) using the new Hidden on Form Pages column on the Data Set details page. 
 Collapsible Event Groups on SOW Characteristics Tab: Users can now collapse and expand event groups on the SOW Characteristics tab, making it easier to navigate complex structures with multiple purchase order lines. 
 Improved Navigation Between Itemized Events and SAP Business Network Workbench: SAP Fieldglass now supports deep linking between itemized events and the Workbench tab in SAP Business Network, allowing Suppliers to move quickly from SOW events to the related Service Entry Sheet (SES) and accelerating invoice completion. 
 Resource Activity Item Enhancements 
 Create Approval Groups for Resources: Buyers can create Approval Groups for Resources submitted by themselves or Suppliers, with the option to define separate groups for labour and equipment, providing greater control over approval workflows. 
 eSignature Activity Item Support for Resource: eSignature Activity Items now support the Resource module, allowing users to initiate and manage DocuSign workflows directly within Resource Activity Items, streamlining document handling and supporting compliance. 
 Resource Activity Item Improvements: Enhancements to Resource Activity Items provide cleaner setup options, clearer task sequencing, and the removal of unsupported configurations, making activity management simpler and more reliable. 
 UX & Platform Improvements 
 The 2026.05 release includes a number of user experience and platform-level improvements that benefit buyers, suppliers, and workers alike. 
 Supplier Statement of Work Dashboard A new Supplier SOW Dashboard provides suppliers with a centralized, real-time view of all SOWs. The dashboard improves visibility into active and pending SOWs, streamlines collaboration between buyers and suppliers through shared insights, improves navigation, reduces manual tracking via external tools, enables faster response times for SOW updates and approvals, and provides greater accuracy in managing deliverables, financials, and compliance. 
 Supplier Ability to View and Download Operational Contract Details A new supplier admin object allows suppliers to view and download contract details — including key terms and rates — ensuring transparency and alignment during service delivery and charge submission. 
 Conclusion 
 The SAP Fieldglass 2026.05 release represents a broad and impactful set of enhancements that collectively advance SAP's vision for intelligent, automated, and compliant external workforce management. Key themes across this release include: 
 AI and automation driving faster sourcing, smarter SOW creation, and conversational requisition workflows via Joule 
 Services Procurement depth through richer Event Hierarchy capabilities, multi-line service confirmations, and tighter S/4HANA integration 
 Compliance and governance improvements for Japanese legislative requirements, contract filtering, and tax code accuracy 
 Supplier empowerment through greater transparency via the SOW Dashboard and operational contract visibility 
 Operational efficiency for administrators through default contract structures, standardized account categories, and improved Resource revision management 
 For organizations looking to maximize the value of this release, the recommended next steps are: 
 Explore the What's New Viewer on the SAP Help Portal for a full interactive overview of all 2026.05 release items. 
 Watch the Release Highlights Video Series — 18 short, focused videos grouped into Contingent Labor, Services Procurement, UX & Universal Updates, and Supplier Updates playlists. 
 Review the 2026.05 Release Spotlight Features Guide available on SAP Community for a curated walkthrough of key innovations. 
 Attend or rewatch the on-demand webinar — Discover What's New in the SAP Fieldglass May 2026 Release — for a guided presentation of key enhancements. 
 The 2026.05 release sets a strong foundation for the remainder of 2026, with further Joule Agent capabilities expected in the coming months. Now is the ideal time to assess your current configuration, engage your implementation partner, and plan adoption of the features most relevant to your external workforce program. 
 Until the next one – best Regards, 
 Fabian 
 For questions or support related to the 2026.05 release, submit a case through SAP for Me or the SAP Fieldglass Help Center.

items.title: Enforcing Minimum Rest Period at Record Save in SAP SuccessFactors Time Tracking
items.author: UditKhera
items.text:
The EU Working Time Directive mandates a minimum 11-hour rest between two consecutive working periods. SAP SuccessFactors Time Tracking supports Rest Rules that highlight violations on the timesheet and can block submission ( KBA 3323455 ). 
 But both act at the timesheet level . The employee can save non-compliant entries all week - and only find out at submission. What if we block it right when they hit Save? 
 The Idea 
 Two building blocks: 
 A valuation step that writes each day’s actual clock-in/clock-out into a Time Container . 
 A validation rule on the Time Recording Profile that reads adjacent days from that container on every save, calculates the rest gap, and raises a hard error if it falls below the threshold. Fig. 1 - Solution Architecture Diagram 
 Building Block 1: The Time Container 
 We need the validation rule to know when the employee actually started and stopped working on adjacent days. A Time Container makes this possible. 
 Input Group 
 A time type group containing all attendance types that count as actual working time. Fig. 2 - Attendance time type group and its members 
 Output Group 
 A time type group with Time Container Type = Yes . This is what the rule will query. Fig. 3 - Output group with Time Container Type enabled 
 Valuation Step 
 Aggregate Input Groups and Split, Valuate Per Day, Threshold = 0. All attendance records are aggregated into the container, storing the earliest start and latest end per employee per day. Fig. 4 - Aggregation valuation step 
 Building Block 2: The Validation Rule 
 A business rule assigned as a Validation Rule on the Time Recording Profile. It fires on every record save. 
 Variables 
 The rule uses Lookup(Time Container) to fetch the previous day’s end time and the next day’s start time. Current-day times come from the record being saved. Fig. 5 - Variable definitions: Time Container lookups and date arithmetic 
 Backward Check - Previous Day 
 Did the employee rest enough between yesterday’s last clock-out and today’s clock-in? 
 The rule calculates the gap in seconds. If < 39,600 (11 hours) - error, save blocked. 
 An overnight detection is built in: if the previous day’s end time is numerically smaller than its start time, the shift crossed midnight, and the DateTime construction adjusts the calendar date accordingly. Fig. 6 - Previous-day rest gap check with overnight handling 
 Forward Check - Next Day 
 If tomorrow is already recorded, does today’s clock-out leave enough rest before tomorrow’s clock-in? 
 Same logic, reversed direction. Same overnight handling. Fig. 7 - Next-day rest gap check with overnight handling 
 The Error “A minimum rest period of 11 hours is required between two working periods. Please review and adjust your time entries.” 
 Raised with Error severity - the record cannot be saved. 
 Quick Example 
 Monday Tuesday 
 Saved entry 08:00 - 19:00 04:00 - 12:00 
 Rest gap 19:00 → 04:00 = 9 hours 
 Result Saved Blocked (< 11 hours) 
 Employee adjusts Tuesday to 06:00 - 12:00 (gap = 11h). Save succeeds. 
 At a Glance 
 Standard Rest Rules This Approach 
 Blocks at Timesheet submission Record save 
 Feedback End of period Immediate 
 The two are complementary - standard rest rules for visual indicators, this approach for hard enforcement at entry. 
 Worth Noting 
 The rule checks against already saved adjacent days. If the adjacent day has not been recorded yet, the lookup returns null and the check is skipped. 
 39,600 seconds = 11 hours. Adjust to match your regulation. 
 Test overnight shifts thoroughly - they are the trickiest edge case.

items.title: Bulk upload of HRMS-Assignment in SAP PM Work Center
items.author: A_Siva-07
items.text:
Introduction 
 While working in one of Project, there was a requirement to assign multiple HR persons to a work center. When the number of assignments is small, these can be maintained manually. However, when there are many work centers and multiple persons to be assigned to each work center, performing the activity manually can be time-consuming. In this scenario, LSMW can be used to automate the assignment. 
 In this blog, I will explain one approach to handle the LSMW recording when the same field name, `SHORT`, is used for both the HR work center object abbreviation and the persons being assigned. 
 The requirement was to assign multiple HR persons to a PM work center using LSMW. During the batch input recording, I noticed that the field name `SHORT` was used for both 
 - The HR work center/object abbreviation. 
 - The persons that need to be assigned to the work center. 
 As the same field name was appearing multiple times, it was needed to differentiate the fields in the LSMW source structure. LSMW Recording 
 Create a LSMW and do the recording. After Batch input recording, make as default all. The first field name `SHORT` represented the HR work center/object abbreviation, while the subsequent `SHORT` fields represented the persons to be assigned. As the same field name was generated multiple times, I changed the names of the fields corresponding to the persons. 
 For the persons to be assigned, I changed the field names as SHORT_1, SHORT_2, SHORT_3 and so on based on the number of persons to be uploaded 

 After defining the source fields, the corresponding fields can be mapped to the recorded fields in the LSMW field mapping step. This allows the same `SHORT` field from the recording to be handled as separate source fields in LSMW. 

 Based on the above structure, the source file can contain the work center and the persons to be assigned, 

 Execute the LSMW steps. Once the mapping and conversion rules are completed, the normal LSMW processing steps can be followed: Mapping: 
 Once the source fields are defined auto field mapping is done, it gets automatically mapped to the edited source fields 
 1. Read Data 
 This step reads the legacy/source data from an external file, such as a CSV, TXT, or tab-delimited file, into LSMW. This step allows to check the data that LSMW has read from the source file. 
 2. Display Read Data 
 This step allows to check the data that LSMW has read from the source file. 
 3. Convert Data 
 In this step, LSMW converts the source data into the format required by SAP and this is where the field mapping and conversion rules defined earlier are applied. 
 4. Display Converted Data 
 This step allows to check the converted data before creating the batch input session. 
 5. Create Batch Input Session 
 Once the converted data looks correct, LSMW creates a Batch Input Session and the session contains the data that will be processed through the SAP transaction. 
 6. Process the Batch Input Session 
 Finally, the batch input session is processed, SAP executes the relevant transaction using the data stored in the session. 
 After processing the session, the HR persons should be assigned to the respective PM work centers. The main challenge in this scenario was that `SHORT` was used for different purposes in the batch input recording. Conclusion 
 LSMW can be useful for mass assignments in SAP PM, especially when the same activity needs to be repeated for a large number of work centers. In this case, renaming the duplicate 'SHORT' fields after using Default All provided a simple way to distinguish the work center object abbreviation from the multiple HR persons being assigned.

Introduction 
 For the years 2026 to 2028, Professor Uta Mathis and Professor Stefan Stöckler will jointly serve as co-chairs of the SAP Academic Board for the DACH region. In the following interview, they explain their motivation, goals, and ideas for further developing the academic community. 
 “Hello Uta, hello Stefan. Could you please both briefly introduce yourselves?” 
 Uta Mathis (UM): “I am a professor of ERP systems and process management at Esslingen University of Applied Sciences, and I have been active in the SAP ecosystem for more than 25 years. As the contact person for the use of SAP in teaching and as the university’s international relations officer, I focus in particular on international partnerships, student exchanges, and co-teaching projects. It is important to me to inspire students to explore the connections between business processes, technology, and practical application.” 

 Stefan Stöckler (SS): “I am a professor of business information systems at the Institute for Information and Process Management at the Ostschweizer Fachhochschule (OST). Before that, I worked in public administration and industry, including as head of SAP development and competence centers. My areas of focus include ERP systems, process management, requirements engineering, and IT management. Together, we combine academic depth, practical experience, and international networks to help develop the SAP community in the DACH region.” 

 SAP Academic Community Conference DACH 2026, von OST – Ostschweizer Fachhochschule und HES-SO Valais-Wallis – https://sapacc26.ost.ch Fotograf: Fabio Schober 
 "What motivates you to serve on the DACH Academic Board?" 
 UM: “I am motivated by the conviction that universities can create great value by sharing experiences, materials, and teaching concepts. I would like to contribute my many years of experience with SAP in teaching, international partnerships, and co-teaching models, and help us jointly develop innovative, practice-oriented approaches.” 
 SS: “To me, the DACH region is an important education and research network with a particular responsibility for topics such as ERP, process management, and digital transformation. I would like to contribute my experience from industry and public administration and work with the members to launch concrete projects that provide lasting support for educators, students, and industry.” 

 "What are your goals for the next two years?" 
 UM: “We would like to establish regular, structured opportunities for discussion on topics such as ‘SAP in Teaching,’ process management, requirements engineering, and digitalization. These will include workshops, webinars, and discussion groups. We also want to develop a digital DACH Academic Board portal and a shared best-practice guide to using SAP in teaching.” 
 SS: “Another priority is promoting collaboration between universities, particularly through co-teaching and COIL projects. We also plan to hold at least one practice-oriented DACH Academic Board workshop per semester and launch a joint research or practical project with SAP or an industry partner. We will raise the Academic Board’s profile through publications, professional events, and social media.” 
 "How do you plan to work with other educators across the DACH region?" 
 SS: “We are committed to open, participatory, and practice-oriented collaboration. Regular events, such as virtual ‘Lunch & Learn’ sessions, will give educators the opportunity to present projects, share experiences, and receive feedback. Clear digital channels—such as a newsletter, wiki, or Miro board—will also make it easier to access materials and information.” 
 UM: “We would also like to encourage agile working groups focused on specific topics, such as integrating SAP into teaching or using COIL models in process management. Educators from different types of institutions and regions should be involved. It is also important to us to support colleagues through mentoring, feedback, and recognition. Our aim is to create a community where educators feel seen, heard, and valued.” 

 "What ideas do you have for working with other Academic Boards and with SAP?" 
 UM: “We see great potential in building international connections with other Academic Boards, including those in EMEA, Ibero-America, North America, Sub-Saharan Africa, Asia Pacific, Japan, and Greater China. Possible initiatives include joint research projects, exchange forums, and COIL modules in which students from different countries work together on real-world business processes.” 
 SS: “Together with SAP and the University Competence Centers, we would like to develop shared teaching and learning materials, such as case studies and learning journeys; organize SAP Days and Challenge Days at universities; and use SAP technologies as a platform for joint projects. The facilities at Esslingen University of Applied Sciences and OST—such as the Low Code Lab and the SmartFactory@OST learning factory—could also be used for practical projects and professional development opportunities for educators.” 
 "Looking back on 2026–2028 in two years, how will you know your work has been successful?" 
 SS: “Our work will have been successful if the DACH Academic Board has become a vibrant, increasingly self-organizing community. That requires established formats for exchange that members actively use, as well as concrete collaborations between universities—for example, co-teaching and COIL projects that continue beyond 2026–2028.” 
 UM: “Another measure of success would be a jointly developed guide or teaching module on ‘SAP in Teaching’ or ‘Process Management in Higher Education’ that is used at several universities. Visible outcomes of international collaboration with SAP and other Academic Boards are just as important. Ultimately, what matters to us is hearing educators say: ‘I found new ideas, met new colleagues, and felt valued in the community.’” 
 Many thanks to Uta Mathis and Stefan Stöckler for the conversation and for sharing their plans for the SAP University Alliance Academic Board in the DACH region. The years 2026 to 2028 offer many opportunities to strengthen connections between universities, integrate SAP topics into higher education and teaching in a practical way, and build new partnerships both within the DACH region and internationally. 
 As the person responsible for the SAP Academic Partnerships program in DACH, I look forward to actively shaping this journey together with the DACH Academic Board and educators.

items.title: Joule Studio with JEV at the Decision Boundary for Autonomous Enterprise AI Agents
items.author: carlosbasto
items.text:
Before we start: this is an independent technical experiment, not an official SAP recommendation. I use “Joule Studio 2.0” for the generation of Joule Studio used here. The SAP documentation supplied for this implementation describes these pro-code capabilities as Early Adopter Care features; commands, interfaces, and availability may change before general availability. JEV is also a newly released technology. All invoice and vendor data in this demonstration is mocked. Releasing a block makes an invoice eligible for subsequent payment; it does not itself execute a payment. 

 1 What this implementation is trying to solve 
 Agentic AI changes the risk profile of an application as soon as the model can call tools with side effects. Reading an invoice, searching vendor history, or summarizing a mismatch are relatively low-impact operations. Clearing a payment block is different: it changes the state of a financial process and can make an invoice eligible for a later payment run. 
 That is the decision point we’ll explore in this article. We will build a supplier-invoice triage agent using Claude Code, the jl CLI, Joule Studio 2.0, and JEV from TypeSafe AI. The agent gathers evidence and decides how to handle the case. Before its release tool can execute, a Python wrapper checks the evidence again and asks JEV for a constrained decision. 
 The generative model handles the conversation, tool orchestration, and explanation. JEV evaluates the proposed action. Ordinary Python maps the result to execution, review, or denial. This makes the transition from reasoning to business action explicit in the implementation and reduces reliance on unconstrained generative output by restricting the consequential decision to predefined outcomes that are enforced in application code. 

 We will go through the concepts, the development setup, the invoice scenario, and the main pieces of code, then build the solution and inspect its behavior in Joule Studio. 

 2 The technologies behind the implementation 
 2.1 Joule Studio pro-code development and the jl CLI 
 SAP documents pro-code development as a way to build Joule Studio solutions from a local IDE and terminal, using the jl CLI and optionally an AI coding agent. The documented workflow covers intent, requirements, specification, solution generation, testing, and deployment. The resulting solution remains source code that developers can inspect and extend. 
 The CLI connects the local workspace to the Joule Studio landscape. It initializes the coding-agent integration, validates the solution structure, packages the assets, and provides deployment and diagnostic commands. Claude Code works inside that environment to read the platform guidance and implement the solution. 
 There are two separate uses of AI here. Claude Code is the development tool. The deployed invoice agent has its own runtime model configuration, business tools, and execution logic. Claude Code does not become a service inside the deployed agent. 
 For the platform workflow, see SAP’s Create an Agent with the CLI and Pro-Code Workflow . 
 2.2 JEV and TypeSafe System One models 
 TypeSafe AI is the company, JEV is its model, and System One is the model category it introduces. TypeSafe announced JEV on 15 September 2026 as its first public System One model, initially in early access. 
 The design centers on a particular consumer: software. An application supplies state and typed questions, and receives answers that it can use directly in its control flow. For this project, the relevant answer is one of four values: allow , confirm , review , or deny . 
 This is more than asking for a nicely formatted response. In its System One documentation , TypeSafe describes models built for constrained judgments and probabilities, without generating a written explanation. The output space is part of the question definition. The application knows which branches it must handle before making the request. 
 That fits the release tool well. By the time release is proposed, the application has already collected business evidence. It needs a judgment about a specific action, followed by a predictable software response. The agent’s LLM remains responsible for explaining the case to the user. 
 2.3 The three TypeSafe primitives 
 TypeSafe exposes three primitives. The introduction and the individual primitive documentation explain their contracts. 

 Primitive 
 What it asks 
 What code receives 

 Choice 
 Which predefined option applies 
 A choice, probabilities, and confidence 

 Score 
 Where the state falls on an ordered rubric 
 A score, probabilities, and confidence 

 Noul 
 Whether a proposition is true 
 A value from 0 to 1 

 Choice naturally fits routing and branching. Score supports ranking or threshold-based behavior. Noul provides a probabilistic answer to a yes/no-style question. In this agent’s running request path, the release guard and completion check both use Choice. 
 The TypeSafe name should not be read as a guarantee of a correct business decision. A constrained answer can still be wrong. The useful contract is that application code can handle the defined outcomes explicitly, while evaluations determine how well the model judges the underlying cases. 
 2.4 Calibration and structured state 
 TypeSafe calls its training approach Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions , or RLCD. Its launch article describes an architecture and training objective focused on producing decisions with useful uncertainty estimates. 
 For Choice and Score, confidence is derived from the returned probability distribution. It is not simply a verbal claim that the model is certain, and it should not be assumed to equal the probability of the selected option. Noul does not have a separate confidence field. TypeSafe’s confidence documentation explains how applications can use this information to choose between automatic action, additional verification, and human review. 
 Calibration is measured across sets of predictions; it does not guarantee an individual answer. Thresholds therefore need evaluation on the application’s own cases. Later in the walkthrough, we will see that this implementation preserves confidence but does not impose a confidence threshold on release. 
 The other useful concept is state . State can be a string, a JSON object, or an array. It carries the material being evaluated; the question separately defines the judgment requested. JEV currently accepts text and structured text data, not invoice images. See TypeSafe’s State documentation . 
 In our implementation, that state describes the proposed tool call, its arguments, evidence summaries, policy, side effects, and reversibility. JEV does not connect to SAP to discover these facts. Our application supplies them. 
 2.5 Small judgments composed in software 
 TypeSafe recommends narrowly scoped questions and composition in code. Independent questions can share one state in a batched request, but one answer does not automatically become the input to another question in that batch. 
 Here, the runtime uses one focused release question after Python has assembled the risk context. This is a practical entry point for experimenting with System One models inside an agent: a named action, a defined answer space, and explicit consequences for every answer. 
 JEV is new enough that I would treat this as an architectural direction to evaluate, rather than a settled standard. What makes it interesting is the possibility of composing specialized model judgments inside ordinary software, while retaining the flexibility of an agent around them. 

 3 Development approach from intent to a Joule Studio solution 
 3.1 Prepare the development environment 
 You need access to a Joule Studio landscape with the relevant pro-code capabilities, a local Claude Code installation, and access to TypeSafe’s API. SAP’s EAC guide specifies Node.js 24 or later for the CLI. The mock scenario does not require a live S/4HANA connection, although the deployed agent still needs its platform-provided runtime model access. 
 Use SAP’s Pro-Code Setup and Anthropic’s Claude Code quickstart for installation and access prerequisites. The EAC CLI installation command in the SAP guide used for this project is: npm install -g @SAP /joule-work-dev-cli-early-adopters@latest
jl v 
 This is an EAC installation pattern, not a promise of a permanently available public npm package. Follow the package access instructions for your landscape and check the current SAP guide before installing. 
 In Joule Studio, open your user settings, go to Develop , and copy the personal Sign-in URL under CLI Authorization . Pass it to the CLI in quotes: jl login '<your Sign-in URL>'
cd supplier-invoice-triage-agent
jl init claude 
 If the folder does not exist yet, then use: mkdir supplier-invoice-triage-agent
cd supplier-invoice-triage-agent
jl init claude 
 jl init claude installs the Joule Studio development skills and creates the MCP configuration used by Claude Code. The coding agent can then work with platform-specific guidance and development tools from this workspace. SAP’s AI Coding Agent documentation explains this integration. 

 3.2 Define the business intent and refine the implementation 
 I used an iterative pro-code workflow. After initializing the workspace, I worked with Claude Code to review and refine the invoice-triage implementation inside the Joule Studio project. The focus was on validating the business behavior, the local test tools, the JEV integration, and the deployable solution structure against the intended design. 
 The implementation starts from a concise business and technical intent: Build a Joule Studio agent that triages a blocked supplier invoice. It must retrieve invoice and matching evidence, check recent invoices from the same vendor, and either release the payment block, create an AP-clerk task, or escalate.

Use local test data for the business tools.

Before any release executes:
- reconstruct the relevant invoice and vendor-history evidence;
- evaluate the proposed release with TypeSafe JEV;
- use a Choice decision with allow, confirm, review, or deny;
- and enforce the result in Python so that only an explicit allow can reach the original release tool. 
 Rather than treating this as a one-shot code-generation exercise, I used Claude Code as a development and review partner. The implementation was inspected against the requirements, with particular attention to the files that define the runtime behavior: 
 app/agent.py 
 app/agent_executor.py 
 app/decision_gates.py 
 app/jev.py 
 app/mcp_providers/agw.py 
 mcp-mock.json 
 asset.yaml

 The review focuses on a few concrete questions: 
 Does the agent retrieve the invoice and recent vendor history before proposing a release? 
 Is release_payment_block actually wrapped before the agent receives the tool? 
 Does the wrapper reconstruct evidence independently of the LLM reasoning? 
 Is JEV called with the intended allow , confirm , review , and deny decision space? 
 Do missing, failed, disabled, or invalid JEV decisions hold the release instead of allowing it through? 
 Does only an explicit allow invoke the original release coroutine? 
 This is the important part of the pro-code workflow: Claude Code can help generate, inspect, and refine the implementation, but the resulting source remains normal application code that can be reviewed against explicit business and technical requirements.
