items.title: Devtoberfest Leaderboard: A Few Observations and Ideas
items.author: Foxi
items.text:
Hi Devtoberfest team, 
 First of all, I really appreciate that we now have a live leaderboard for Devtoberfest! It's a great addition that makes the event even more engaging and adds a fun competitive element. 🙂 
 While checking the leaderboard, I noticed a few things that I thought might be worth sharing as ideas for possible future improvements. 
 1. Ranking participants with equal scores 
 To illustrate what I mean, here's a concrete example from my own position on the leaderboard: At one point, I had 29,415 points and was ranked #2, with only one participant ahead of me at 29,420 points. As more participants reached 29,420 points, I naturally moved down the leaderboard. Once six participants had 29,420 points, I would have expected my 29,415 points to put me at #7. 
 However, as additional participants reached the same 29,415 points, my position continued to move down as well, eventually to #13. 
 The exact numbers aren't important here. They simply illustrate the behavior I noticed: when participants have the same score, their relative positions don't seem to remain stable. 
 Two possible approaches to handling equal scores come to mind: 
 First come, first served: Participants who reach a particular score first retain their position ahead of participants who reach the same score later. 
 Shared ranking: Participants with identical scores share the same rank. In the example above, all six participants with 29,420 points would share rank #1, while those with 29,415 points would share rank #7. 
 Either approach could make the handling of equal scores more transparent and predictable. 
 2. Exploring the full leaderboard 
 I'd also love to be able to browse the entire leaderboard rather than just the top-ranked participants. It would be interesting to explore the lower ranks and see how other participants are doing. Perhaps pagination or a "Load more" option could make this possible. 
 3. Total number of active participants 
 Another nice addition would be a counter showing the total number of participants who have earned points. It would give us a better sense of how many developers are actively taking part in Devtoberfest. 
 Just a few observations! 
 Of course, I know that leaderboard positions don't affect the final prize distribution. This isn't about fairness or prizes. It's simply about making the leaderboard experience even more enjoyable. 
 Having a live leaderboard in the first place is already a great addition to Devtoberfest, and these are just a few observations and ideas for possible improvements. 🙂 
 What do you think? Would any of these improvements make sense for the leaderboard?

deep_dives.title: Draft Query Views: The RAP Security Gap Nobody Checks
deep_dives.explanation:
Ref 9 exposes an architectural blind spot in RAP that catches out even experienced developers: `DCL` authorization checks defined via `@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #CHECK` on your active CDS entity do **not** automatically apply to the corresponding draft persistence table. RAP's draft-enabled apps store in-progress edits in a separate draft table, generated alongside the active table, and by default that draft table has no independent access control layer. A user who cannot see or edit certain active records can still create, view, and edit a draft of those same records unless you explicitly close the gap.

The fix is a `Draft Query View`: a CDS view built specifically over the draft persistence, wired into the behavior definition via the query addition alongside `use draft;`. This gives you a second, independent point to apply `@AccessControl.authorizationCheck` — meaning your DCL role now protects both the active and draft states of the entity. Without it, the projection layer's authorization is effectively a facade during the edit-in-progress phase.

The post walks through a complete, non-trivial example: a `Price Change Request` app starting from the database table `zaf_dt_pricerequ`, through the interface CDS entity `ZAF_I_PRICEREQU` (carrying the `@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #CHECK` annotation), the projection `ZAF_C_PRICEREQDF` (using `provider contract transactional_query`), and a behavior definition wiring in the standard draft actions — `Activate`, `Discard`, `Edit`, `Resume`, `Prepare`. Metadata extensions (`@UI.facet`, `@UI.lineItem`, `@UI.identification`) complete the Fiori Elements rendering.

For teams building transactional RAP apps with sensitive data — pricing, HR, credit — this is not an edge case. Any draft-enabled business object with row-level or field-level authorization requirements needs this pattern verified explicitly, because the framework will silently let it slide otherwise. Treat draft query views as a mandatory checklist item in RAP security reviews, not an optional hardening step.

Draft Query Views and the `use draft;` behavior directive

deep_dives.title: X.509 Certificate Authentication for the ABAP ODBC Driver: PEM vs PSE
deep_dives.explanation:
Ref 34 is a dense, code-heavy walkthrough of certificate-based auth for the SAP ODBC driver — increasingly the default for password-less connections into ABAP systems, particularly on BTP. The core parameter is `AuthenticationType=X509`; once set, `Uid` becomes unnecessary because the certificate itself carries the identity. The driver supports two distinct certificate handling models, and confusing them is the most common configuration mistake: `PEM`, where the driver itself parses and manages the certificate material, and `PSE` (Personal Security Environment), the SAP-standard format managed at the OS level via `sapcryptolib` and the `sapgenpse` tool.

A critical, easy-to-miss detail: the `TrustedCertificates` and `UserCertificates` connection parameters work together as a combined set, but the driver only uses the *first* private key it encounters — if your connection string lists multiple certificates with private keys, only the first is honored. This has bitten teams who assumed multiple client certs could be chained.

Patch Level 33 is the milestone to know: it introduced file-path support for PEM certificates (previously you had to inline the full PEM content in the connection string, which broke under `unixODBC`'s string length limits) and added support for encrypted private keys, with the decryption password passed via the standard `Pwd` parameter. For PSE-based setups, the driver defers entirely to OS-level credential management: it requires the `SECUDIR` environment variable pointing to the PSE store and a `cred_v2` credential file, both provisioned via `sapgenpse`.

For any developer setting up secure external tool integration (BI tools, custom reporting, third-party connectors) into an ABAP system without embedding passwords, this is the reference architecture. Know which format your target environment expects before you start — retrofitting from PEM to PSE (or vice versa) mid-project means redoing your entire credential provisioning pipeline.
key_concepts: PEM (driver-managed) vs PSE (OS-managed via `sapcryptolib`) certificate models
`TrustedCertificates`/`UserCertificates` parameter semantics — first private key only
Patch Level 33: file-path support and encrypted private key handling

deep_dives.title: Joule Studio's JEV Model: Separating Judgment from Generation in Agentic AI
deep_dives.explanation:
Ref 40 describes a production architecture pattern worth studying regardless of whether you use Joule Studio: separating the *generative* reasoning layer from the *decision* layer when an AI agent's output triggers a real side effect (in this case, releasing a payment). The invoice triage agent uses Claude for evidence gathering, tool orchestration, and natural-language explanation — the parts of the task that benefit from open-ended reasoning — but hands the actual release-or-hold decision to `JEV`, TypeSafe's constrained judgment model.

JEV exposes three primitives instead of free text: `Choice` (pick from a predefined option set), `Score` (rank against a rubric), and `Noul` (a calibrated yes/no probability). Crucially, JEV is trained with `RLCD` (Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions), which produces confidence scores derived from actual probability distributions — not a language model's verbal self-assessment of certainty, which is notoriously unreliable. The output of JEV is then passed to a plain Python wrapper that enforces the outcome deterministically before any state-changing call is made; the LLM never directly executes the side effect.

This three-layer separation — generative model for evidence and explanation, decision model for bounded judgment, imperative code for enforcement — is the practical answer to 'how do you let an agent make consequential decisions without letting it run wild.' The `jl` CLI supports this as a pro-code workflow: build and test locally in your own IDE (the post specifically uses Claude Code), then push to the Joule Studio landscape for validation, packaging, and deployment.

On the data side, the agent's memory is handled through SAP HANA Cloud's `VECTOR_EMBEDDING` and `COSINE_SIMILARITY` SQL functions, scoped by `agentID` and `invokerID`, so semantic retrieval only pulls relevant history into the prompt rather than replaying the full conversation — keeping both token cost and latency under control. For architects evaluating agentic AI for anything touching financial or irreversible actions, this pattern — generate, judge, enforce — is the one to bring to the design review.
key_concepts: Separating generative reasoning from constrained decision-making in agentic AI
JEV judgment primitives: Choice, Score, Noul
RLCD-calibrated confidence vs verbal LLM certainty
Deterministic outcome enforcement in code before side effects execute
Semantic memory scoping via `VECTOR_EMBEDDING`/`COSINE_SIMILARITY` in HANA Cloud

trending_problems.theme: Extension frameworks that display data but silently fail to persist it
trending_problems.description: Two separate reports (ref 49: BDT custom field on BP Credit Segment, ref 30: inbound IDoc field case conversion) show the same underlying pattern — a custom field is correctly configured, visible in the UI, and even accessible at the code level, but something in the framework's internal buffer/processing chain drops or transforms it before it reaches the database.
trending_problems.teaching_tip: Frame this as a 'trust but verify persistence' exercise: never assume a field that displays and is readable in a PAI/PBO handler has actually completed the round trip to the database. Trace the full path from UI to table for any custom field before signing off.

trending_problems.theme: AI coding agents underdeliver on real ABAP development tasks
trending_problems.description: Ref 13 documents a hands-on test of AI agents (via VSCode ABAP-MCP with multiple models) attempting real ABAP development in a transport-based, non-gCTS environment: agents ignored the MCP tool server, defaulted to file creation instead of using proper SAP tooling, produced duplicate unit tests, and required as much manual rework as writing the code from scratch. Only reliable use case found: code explanation.
trending_problems.teaching_tip: Use this as a grounded counterweight to AI hype in your community — have developers benchmark an AI agent against a real ticket and time both paths honestly before adopting agentic workflows into their process.

trending_problems.theme: IDE and tooling update sequencing breaks developer environments
trending_problems.description: Ref 3 shows that Eclipse's own update mechanism — not ADT — pulls incompatible `org.objectweb.asm` bundle versions when 2026-09 exists alongside a 2026-06 install, breaking IDE startup entirely. The only safe path is a specific update sequence (disable SAP's update site, update Eclipse platform first, re-enable and update ADT after).
trending_problems.teaching_tip: Turn this into a checklist exercise: before any Eclipse platform update, always disable third-party update sites first, verify platform update completes cleanly, then re-enable and update tool-specific sites separately.

trending_problems.theme: iPaaS/integration platforms produce inconsistent data shapes at scale boundaries
trending_problems.description: Ref 25 shows SAP Integration Suite's XML-to-JSON converter silently changing output type — array for multiple elements, plain object for a single element — breaking any consumer that assumes a stable array contract. This is a classic 'works until the edge case' integration bug.
trending_problems.teaching_tip: Have developers write integration test cases that specifically cover zero, one, and many occurrences of repeating XML elements before any XML-to-JSON conversion goes to production.

trending_problems.theme: BTP authentication model diverges from on-premise assumptions
trending_problems.description: Ref 20 shows a VSCode Fiori Generator failing to authenticate to BTP ABAP Environment OData catalog services (401 on V4) even though the same user succeeds via browser — and existing on-premise S/4HANA workarounds don't apply because BTP's OAuth flow is architecturally different from traditional ABAP authentication.
trending_problems.teaching_tip: When troubleshooting BTP tooling auth failures, always separate 'browser session succeeded' from 'API/programmatic auth succeeded' — they use different token flows and debugging one doesn't validate the other.

trending_problems.theme: RAP security defaults are more porous than developers assume
trending_problems.description: Ref 9 shows that DCL-based access control on an active CDS entity does not extend to its draft persistence counterpart by default — a gap that is easy to miss because the app appears fully secured at the projection layer.
trending_problems.teaching_tip: Add 'verify draft query view exists and carries authorization checks' as a mandatory line item in any RAP security code review checklist.

post_drafts.title: RAP draft data security gap
post_drafts.text:
*Your DCL access control might not protect draft data in RAP.*

Here's the gap: `@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #CHECK` on your active CDS entity does NOT automatically extend to the draft persistence table.

A user restricted from certain active records can still create/edit a *draft* of those records — unless you add a Draft Query View.

The fix: build a CDS view over the draft table, wire it into the behavior definition alongside `use draft;`, and apply authorization checks there independently.

Ref 9 walks through a complete working example — DB table → interface CDS → projection → behavior definition — for a Price Change Request app.

*Takeaway:* if your RAP app has drafts + sensitive data, don't assume projection-level security is enough. Check the draft layer separately.

https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/securing-draft-data-in-sap-rap-with-draft-query-views/ba-p/14488903

post_drafts.title: Eclipse update PSA
post_drafts.text:
*Eclipse 2026-06 users — read before you update.*

If Eclipse 2026-09 is available and you update ADT first, `org.objectweb.asm` version conflicts can break your IDE startup completely.

This is an Eclipse platform bug, not an ADT bug (SAP note 3806264, upstream equinox/p2 issues linked).

*Safe sequence:*
1. Disable the SAP Development Tools update site
2. Update Eclipse platform to 2026-09
3. Re-enable the SAP site, then Check for Updates for ADT separately

Already broken? Fresh 2026-09 install + reuse your existing workspace preserves everything.

post_drafts.title: HANA Cloud Sept 2026 — AI moves into the database
post_drafts.text:
*SAP HANA Cloud QRC3 (Sept 2026) puts AI directly in SQL.*

Highlights for ABAP/data teams:

• `AI_CORE_REQUEST` — call an LLM straight from a SELECT, or bind it to a generated column for automatic enrichment on every insert/update

• Agent Memory Service — persistent agent context across sessions, scoped by agentID, with semantic retrieval via `VECTOR_EMBEDDING`/`COSINE_SIMILARITY`

• GeoSPARQL — spatial predicates (intersects, within, distance) now native in the Knowledge Graph Engine

• Calculation Views are now discoverable by AI retrieval — natural language queries against your existing analytic models

*Why it matters:* AI-enriched data pipelines with zero application code, fully governed inside the database security layer.

interview_questions.question: In a RAP application with draft capability, you've applied DCL authorization checks on the active CDS entity. Is the draft data automatically protected by the same checks? If not, how do you fix it?
interview_questions.answer: No — DCL access control on the active entity's `@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #CHECK` annotation does not automatically extend to the draft persistence table, because drafts are stored in a physically separate table generated by the draft framework. To close this gap, you need to build a Draft Query View: a CDS view over the draft persistence, wired into the behavior definition's query addition alongside the `use draft;` directive, with its own `@AccessControl.authorizationCheck` annotation. Without this, a user who is restricted from certain active records can still create and edit a draft of those same records, since the draft layer has no independent authorization enforcement by default. This should be a mandatory check in any RAP security review for draft-enabled apps handling sensitive data.

interview_questions.question: You're configuring the ODBC driver for ABAP to use X.509 certificate authentication instead of username/password. What are the two supported certificate handling models, and what changed in Patch Level 33?
interview_questions.answer: The driver supports two models: PEM, where the driver itself parses and manages the certificate material passed via the `TrustedCertificates`/`UserCertificates` connection parameters, and PSE (Personal Security Environment), the SAP-standard format managed at the OS level via `sapcryptolib` and provisioned with the `sapgenpse` tool, requiring the `SECUDIR` environment variable and a `cred_v2` credential file. Patch Level 33 was a key milestone: it added file-path support for PEM certificates, which solved a real production problem where long inline PEM content in connection strings broke under `unixODBC`'s string length limits, and it added support for encrypted private keys, with the decryption password passed via the standard `Pwd` parameter. One subtlety to know: if multiple certificates with private keys are listed, the driver only uses the first one — it doesn't chain multiple client keys.

interview_questions.question: Describe an architecture pattern for letting an AI agent trigger a real, irreversible business action (e.g., releasing a payment) while keeping the decision auditable and bounded.
interview_questions.answer: The pattern separates three distinct layers instead of letting one LLM do everything end-to-end. First, a generative model (e.g., Claude) handles evidence gathering, tool orchestration, and natural-language explanation — open-ended reasoning tasks where flexibility is an asset. Second, a specialized constrained-judgment model (in SAP's case, TypeSafe's JEV) makes the actual decision using bounded primitives — a predefined Choice, a rubric-based Score, or a calibrated yes/no Noul probability — trained via RLCD so its confidence reflects real probability distributions rather than an LLM's self-reported certainty. Third, deterministic code (plain Python, not the LLM) enforces the outcome and executes the side effect only after the constrained decision is returned — the generative model never directly triggers the state change. This generate-judge-enforce separation gives you an explicit, inspectable decision boundary and keeps the risk profile of the system bounded even as the reasoning layer remains flexible.

digest.headline: RAP's draft data has a DCL security gap, an Eclipse update can silently break your IDE, and HANA Cloud QRC3 pushes LLM calls straight into SQL.
digest.overview:
Today's material centers on gaps between what developers assume works and what actually holds up in production. The standout technical piece (ref 9) exposes a real architectural blind spot in RAP: DCL authorization on an active CDS entity does not automatically protect the corresponding draft persistence, and the fix — Draft Query Views — is demonstrated end-to-end with working code. Alongside it, a critical Eclipse update bug (ref 3) and a detailed X.509/ODBC authentication guide (ref 34) round out solid core-stack content, while SAP HANA Cloud's September 2026 release (ref 28) pushes LLM inference and semantic memory directly into SQL.

A second thread runs through several items: extension and integration frameworks that look correct on the surface but fail quietly. A BDT custom field on BP Credit Segment displays but never persists (ref 49); an IDoc field ignores its lowercase domain setting (ref 30); SAP Integration Suite's XML-to-JSON converter silently changes output type between single and multiple records (ref 25); and a hands-on test of AI coding agents in a real transport-based ABAP environment found them unreliable beyond code explanation (ref 13). None of these are exotic — they're the kind of gaps that surface in production only when someone hits the edge case.

top_stories.title: RAP draft data bypasses your DCL authorization checks
top_stories.summary: DCL access control on an active CDS entity does not automatically extend to its draft persistence table. A working Price Change Request example shows the full fix: a Draft Query View wired into the behavior definition, from database table through interface CDS, projection CDS, and metadata extensions.
top_stories.why_it_matters: This is a silent security gap in a widely used RAP pattern — draft-enabled transactional apps. Any team with sensitive data in a draft-capable RAP app needs to verify this explicitly; the framework does not enforce it by default.

top_stories.title: Eclipse 2026-06 → 2026-09 update sequence can brick your IDE
top_stories.summary: Updating ADT while Eclipse 2026-09 exists triggers org.objectweb.asm dependency conflicts that break IDE startup entirely. Root cause is in Eclipse's own update mechanism, not ADT. Safe path: disable SAP's update site, update the platform first, then update ADT separately; a fresh 2026-09 install with workspace reuse recovers broken installs.
top_stories.why_it_matters: A broken IDE halts development outright for every developer on the affected version. This is an operational, not cosmetic, issue with a clear procedural fix.

top_stories.title: SAP HANA Cloud September 2026 (QRC3): LLM calls and agent memory move into SQL
top_stories.summary: New AI_CORE_REQUEST SQL function calls LLMs directly from SELECT statements or generated columns for automatic enrichment. Agent Memory Service adds persistent, semantically-searchable conversation history via VECTOR_EMBEDDING/COSINE_SIMILARITY. GeoSPARQL adds native spatial reasoning to the Knowledge Graph Engine.
top_stories.why_it_matters: Shifts AI integration from application middleware into the database engine, simplifying architecture and keeping governance inside the database security layer — relevant for any team building agentic or data-enrichment pipelines on HANA Cloud.

top_stories.title: Joule Studio's JEV model: separating judgment from generation in agentic AI
top_stories.summary: An invoice triage agent architecture separates evidence-gathering LLM (Claude) from a constrained decision model (TypeSafe JEV, with Choice/Score/Noul primitives and RLCD-calibrated confidence) and enforces the outcome via plain Python before any side effect executes.
top_stories.why_it_matters: A concrete governance pattern for agentic AI touching irreversible business actions — useful reference architecture for anyone evaluating AI agents for financial or state-changing workflows.

top_stories.title: X.509 certificate authentication for the ODBC driver: PEM vs PSE, and what PL 33 fixed
top_stories.summary: Detailed guide to configuring password-less certificate auth for the ABAP ODBC driver, covering both PEM (driver-managed) and PSE (OS-managed via sapcryptolib) formats. Patch Level 33 added file-path support for PEM certs and encrypted private key support, fixing a real production issue with long connection strings under unixODBC.
top_stories.why_it_matters: Essential reference for teams setting up secure external tool integration into ABAP systems without embedded passwords, especially on BTP.

top_stories.title: AI coding agents underdeliver in real on-premise ABAP workflows
top_stories.summary: A hands-on test of AI agents via VSCode ABAP-MCP across multiple models (Claude Haiku, Opus, NVidia Nemotron) found agents ignore the MCP tool server, default to local file creation instead of proper SAP tooling, and produce code requiring as much rework as manual development. Only reliable use case: code explanation.
top_stories.why_it_matters: A grounded counterpoint to AI agent hype, from someone who actually tested it against a real transport-based workflow rather than a demo scenario.

top_stories.title: Custom field configured correctly but never reaches the database
top_stories.summary: A BDT custom field on BP Credit Segment (ZZ_RISK_CLASS) displays in the UI and is accessible in the PAI FM but is cleared on save — no COLLECT function module exists for the dataset, leaving the persistence path unclear (XCHNG/DSAVE events, EEW_PS include, or a BAdI around CL_UKM_ACCOUNT).
top_stories.why_it_matters: A recurring pattern in SAP extensibility: UI-level configuration success does not guarantee persistence. Requires tracing the full internal buffer mechanism, not just the field configuration layer.

top_stories.title: SAP Integration Suite's XML-to-JSON converter changes type based on record count
top_stories.summary: A single XML element converts to a JSON object, while multiple occurrences of the same element correctly convert to an array — breaking any consumer (UI5, mobile, external API) that expects a stable array contract and calls .map() on it.
top_stories.why_it_matters: A silent production failure vector: integrations work until a single-record edge case hits, at which point downstream code breaks without warning.

top_stories.title: VSCode Fiori Generator can't authenticate to BTP ABAP OData catalog despite working browser login
top_stories.summary: The Connection Manager for SAP Systems extension gets a 401 on OData V4 catalog service calls on BTP ABAP Environment, even though the same user authenticates fine via browser. Existing S/4HANA on-premise workarounds don't apply because BTP's OAuth model differs architecturally.
top_stories.why_it_matters: Highlights that browser session success and programmatic API auth success are not equivalent — a common source of confusion when troubleshooting BTP tooling.

top_stories.title: Inbound IDoc custom field ignores lowercase domain setting, converts to uppercase
top_stories.summary: A custom inbound IDoc field with a domain configured for lowercase (and a separate CHAR20 field without a domain) both get converted to uppercase unexpectedly, with the root cause unidentified — likely in IDoc segment definition or standard processing rather than the domain property itself.
top_stories.why_it_matters: IDocs remain critical for SAP data exchange; understanding exactly where in the processing chain type/case conversions occur is essential for data quality in integrations.
